lessons.title: Water Conservation Techniques for Smallholders
lessons.body:
Water is heavy and expensive to move. Before you invest in pumps or pipes, cut your water need in half. Start with mulch: a 5 cm layer of dry grass, maize stover, or wood chips around each plant reduces evaporation by up to 70%. In drylands like Machakos, Kenya, farmers who mulch with crop residues save 40 litres per square metre per season. Next, switch from flooding to drip or pitcher irrigation. A buried clay pot (olla) filled once a week seeps water slowly to roots, using 50â70% less water than surface watering. For row crops, use a simple bucket-drip kit: a 20-litre bucket with 2â3 micro-tubes per plant, hung 1 metre above ground. This costs under $5 and waters 20 plants for two days. 

Water deeply and less often. Shallow daily watering trains roots to stay near the surface where they dry out. Instead, give each plant 5â10 litres twice a week, depending on soil. Sandy soil needs more frequent, smaller doses; clay soil holds water longer but absorbs slowly, so water in two rounds. Check moisture by sticking your finger 5 cm into the soil. If it feels dry, water; if damp, wait. 

Capture every drop. Dig contour trenches or swales on slopes to slow runoff and let it soak in. A 30 cm deep trench along a contour line can store 100 litres per metre of length. In Ethiopia, such trenches increased maize yields by 30% during dry spells. Also, shade your soil with living mulch like sweet potato vines or cowpeas. They cover the ground, reduce evaporation, and fix nitrogen. 

Finally, maintain your system. Fix leaks immediatelyâa dripping joint wastes 15 litres a day. Clean filters and emitters weekly; clogged drip lines waste water and kill plants. Train one family member to check the system every morning. Water conservation is not about doing without; it is about getting more crop per drop.

lessons.title: Using Greywater and Rainwater Safely
lessons.body:
Greywater is water from baths, sinks, and laundry. It can irrigate fruit trees, fodder, and ornamental plants, but not leafy vegetables eaten raw. Never use water from toilets (blackwater) without treatment. A family of six produces 100â200 litres of greywater dailyâenough to water 20 banana plants or 50 square metres of maize. 

To use greywater safely, first filter it. Pass it through a 20-litre bucket with layers of gravel, sand, and charcoal. This removes soap, hair, and grease. Then store it no more than 24 hours; bacteria grow fast in warm climates. Apply it directly to the soil, not leaves, using a watering can or buried perforated pipes. Do not store greywater in open containersâmosquitoes breed there. 

Soap choice matters. Use biodegradable, low-sodium soap like potassium-based or homemade ash soap. Avoid bleach, borax, and strong disinfectants; they kill soil life and burn roots. If using detergent, dilute greywater with fresh water 1:1. 

Rainwater harvesting is cleaner and safer. A 20-square-metre roof in a 600 mm rainfall area collects 12,000 litres per year. That is enough to irrigate a 100-square-metre garden for three months. Use gutters (local bamboo or PVC) to channel water into a 1,000-litre tank or a lined pit. First-flush diverter: discard the first 20 litres of rain to wash off bird droppings and dust. 

For smallholders, a simple ferrocement tank (2,000 litres) costs about $80 and lasts 20 years. In Uganda, farmers using rainwater for drip irrigation grew tomatoes year-round. Always cover tanks to prevent evaporation and mosquito breeding. Test stored rainwater for pH yearly; if below 5.5, add a handful of wood ash per 100 litres. 

Combine greywater and rainwater: use rainwater for vegetables and seedlings, greywater for trees and fodder. This doubles your water supply without extra cost.

lessons.title: Solar-Powered Irrigation for Sustainability
lessons.body:
A solar pump saves money and diesel. A 200-watt solar panel kit (about $250) can pump 1,500 litres per day from a 10-metre deep well or riverâenough to drip-irrigate 0.2 hectares of vegetables. In Kenya, farmers using solar pumps cut irrigation costs by 80% compared to petrol pumps. 

Choose the right pump. For shallow water (under 5 metres), use a surface centrifugal pump. For deeper wells, use a submersible pump. Match pump power to panel size: a 100W panel runs a 0.5 HP pump for 5 hours on a sunny day. You need a controller to protect the pump from dry running and to convert DC to AC if using AC pumps. 

Mount panels facing the equator (north in southern Africa, south in northern Africa) at an angle equal to your latitude. In Malawi (latitude 13Â°S), tilt panels 13Â° north. Keep panels cleanâdust reduces output by 20% in a week. 

Store water, not electricity. Batteries are expensive and wear out. Instead, pump into an elevated tank (2â5 metres high) during the day. Gravity then feeds drip lines. A 1,000-litre tank at 2 metres height gives 0.2 bar pressureâenough for drip but not sprinklers. 

Solar pumps work best with drip irrigation because drip needs low pressure and low flow. Connect a 200W pump to 100 metres of drip tape with emitters every 30 cm. Run the pump from 9am to 3pm when sun is strongest. Use a float switch to stop pumping when tank is full. 

Maintenance: check panel connections monthly, clean panel surface weekly, and inspect pump impeller every 6 months. In Senegal, a womenâs cooperative used a 300W solar pump to irrigate 0.5 ha of onions, earning $1,200 per season. Solar is not just greenâit is cheaper and more reliable than grid or diesel for smallholders.

lessons.title: Organic Fertigation and Compost Tea
lessons.body:
Fertigation means adding nutrients to irrigation water. Organic fertigation uses compost tea, manure tea, or liquid seaweed. It feeds plants directly and saves labour. 

Make compost tea: fill a 200-litre drum with 20 kg of mature compost (no meat, no bones) in a burlap sack. Add 1 kg of molasses or 2 litres of urine to feed microbes. Fill with water, stir daily for 3 days. The tea is ready when it smells earthy, not rotten. Dilute 1:5 with water before applying. Use within 24 hoursâit spoils fast. 

Apply compost tea through drip lines or as a soil drench. For drip, inject 10 litres of tea per 100 litres of water. Flush lines with clear water after each fertigation to prevent clogging. For vegetables, apply every 10 days during growth. For fruit trees, apply 20 litres per tree monthly. 

Manure tea is simpler: put 10 kg of fresh cow manure in a permeable sack in a 200-litre drum of water. Let it steep for 7 days. Dilute 1:10. This is high in nitrogen but can burn young plants, so use on mature crops. 

Urine is a powerful organic fertiliser. Human urine diluted 1:10 with water gives a balanced NPK (about 0.5% N). Apply to maize, cabbage, and bananas. Do not use urine on leafy greens eaten raw within 3 weeks of harvest. 

Seaweed extract: if near the coast, collect seaweed, rinse off salt, and ferment in water for 2 weeks. Dilute 1:20. It provides trace minerals and growth hormones. 

Safety: always wear gloves when handling manure. Wash vegetables after harvest. Do not use manure tea on crops eaten raw. Store teas in shade, covered, to avoid mosquito breeding. 

In Rwanda, farmers using compost tea on tomatoes increased yields by 25% and reduced chemical fertiliser by half. Start with a small drum; scale up as you learn.

lessons.title: Irrigation for Agroforestry and Polycultures
lessons.body:
Agroforestry mixes trees with crops. Polycultures grow many species together. Both need smart irrigation because different plants have different water needs. 

Design your system in zones. Zone 1 (near house): vegetables and herbsâwater daily with drip or watering can. Zone 2: fruit trees and staple cropsâwater twice a week with drip or basin irrigation. Zone 3: timber and fodder treesâwater only in first two years, then rely on rain. 

Use basin irrigation for trees. Dig a 1-metre diameter basin around each tree, 15 cm deep. Fill with 20 litres once a week. Mulch with 10 cm of leaves. This trains roots deep. For young trees, add a 2-litre plastic bottle with a small hole near the baseâslow drip for 3 days. 

For polycultures like maize-beans-squash, use a single drip line down the row. Space emitters every 30 cm. Beans and squash shade the soil, reducing evaporation by 30%. Maize roots go deep, beans fix nitrogen, squash covers ground. Water all together twice a week with 10 litres per metre of row. 

In alley cropping (rows of trees with crops between), plant leucaena or gliricidia trees 4 metres apart. Irrigate the crop rows with drip; the trees send roots under the crops and need no extra water after year two. Prune trees twice a year and use prunings as mulch. 

In drylands, use Zai pits: 20 cm deep, 30 cm wide, filled with manure and compost. Plant one tree or crop per pit. Water each pit with 5 litres every 5 days. Zai pits capture runoff and concentrate water. In Burkina Faso, Zai pits with agroforestry grew sorghum in 300 mm rainfall. 

Maintenance: check emitters for rootsâtree roots can clog drip lines. Flush lines monthly. Prune tree roots that enter drip tape. Use a filter with 120 mesh. 

Irrigating polycultures saves water because diverse roots use water at different depths. A well-designed system uses 40% less water than monoculture. Start with two species, then add more.

lessons.title: Reducing Energy Use in Irrigation
lessons.body:
Pumping water is the biggest energy cost on a small farm. You can cut energy use by half with simple changes. 

First, reduce the height you pump. Every metre of lift costs energy. If you pump from a river 3 metres below and push water 5 metres up, that is 8 metres of head. Move your pump closer to the water source. Use a ramp or dig a sump to lower the pump. 

Second, use gravity. Fill a tank on a hill or a raised platform (2â5 metres high) during off-peak hours or when solar is available. Then let gravity feed drip lines. A 2-metre high tank gives 0.2 barâenough for drip. This eliminates pumping during irrigation. 

Third, choose low-pressure emitters. Standard drip tape runs at 1 bar. Low-pressure tape runs at 0.5 bar. You can use a 12-volt pump or even a hand pump to pressurise. In Zimbabwe, farmers using low-pressure drip with a 50W solar panel irrigated 0.1 ha. 

Fourth, irrigate at dawn or dusk. Midday heat causes 30% evaporation loss. Watering in the evening lets soil absorb water overnight. Also, avoid pumping when wind is strongâevaporation increases. 

Fifth, maintain your pump. A clogged impeller or worn bearings increase energy use by 20%. Clean the impeller every 3 months. Check for leaks in pipesâa 1 mm hole wastes 20 litres per hour and drops pressure. 

Sixth, use a timer or float switch. Do not run the pump longer than needed. A float switch turns off the pump when the tank is full. A timer runs the pump for 1 hour instead of 3. 

Seventh, consider a treadle pump for very small plots (under 0.1 ha). It costs $50 and uses human energy, but it is zero fuel. For larger plots, a solar pump with a 100W panel and a 500-litre tank can irrigate 0.2 ha with no fuel cost. 

In Ethiopia, farmers who switched from diesel to solar and gravity cut energy costs from $100 to $5 per season. Start by measuring your current energy useâthen apply one change at a time.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Sustainable and Organic Irrigation Practices for African Smallholders

This practical reference consolidates the core techniques covered in the module â water conservation, greywater and rainwater use, solar-powered irrigation, organic fertigation, agroforestry irrigation, and energy reduction â into a single working document you can use in the field or in a business plan. It is written for smallholder farmers, extension officers, and agribusiness advisors operating in sub-Saharan Africa, where rainfall is increasingly erratic, energy costs are rising, and market buyers are paying premiums for certified organic and water-efficient produce.

1. Water Conservation Techniques for Smallholders

Water conservation is the highest-return investment for most African smallholders because it reduces both pumping costs and crop failure risk. The most effective field-level techniques are:

  • Mulching with crop residues, grass, or plastic film to cut evaporation by 30â50%.
  • Zai pits and planting basins (common in the Sahel) to capture and concentrate rainfall.
  • Tied ridges and contour bunds to slow runoff and increase infiltration.
  • Deficit irrigation on drought-tolerant crops such as sorghum, millet, and cowpea.
  • Drip and micro-sprinkler systems instead of furrow or flood irrigation.

For a commercial smallholder, the business case is straightforward: a 1-hectare drip kit typically costs USD 500â1,500 and can cut water use by 40â60% while raising marketable yield by 20â50% for vegetables. Payback is often one to two seasons.

2. Using Greywater and Rainwater Safely

Greywater (from kitchens, baths, and laundry) and rainwater harvesting can supplement irrigation, especially in peri-urban and dryland farming. However, both carry contamination risks that must be managed.

Rainwater harvesting options include roof catchment tanks, rock catchments, sand dams, and farm ponds lined with clay or HDPE. A 100 mÂ² roof in a 600 mm rainfall zone can yield roughly 50,000 litres per year â enough to irrigate 0.1â0.2 ha of vegetables through drip.

Greywater should be filtered, settled, and applied to non-leafy crops or through subsurface drip. Never use greywater containing bleach, borax, or high-salt detergents on vegetables eaten raw.

3. Solar-Powered Irrigation for Sustainability

Solar photovoltaic (PV) pumping has transformed smallholder irrigation economics across Africa. A 500 Wp panel with a DC surface pump can lift water from a shallow well or river to a 2â5 m head at 3,000â6,000 litres per day â sufficient for 0.25â0.5 ha of drip-irrigated vegetables. Compared with diesel pumps, solar systems eliminate fuel costs (often 30â50% of operating expenses) and require minimal maintenance.

Key design rules: size the pump to the dry-season water source, not the wet-season peak; use a float switch or timer to avoid over-pumping; and protect panels from theft and dust. For larger farms, hybrid solar-diesel or solar-grid systems balance reliability and cost.

4. Organic Fertigation and Compost Tea

Fertigation delivers dissolved nutrients through the irrigation stream. Organic fertigation uses compost tea, vermicompost leachate, or fermented plant extracts instead of synthetic fertiliser. This suits organic certification and improves soil biology.

Compost tea recipe (smallholder scale): mix 10 kg mature compost with 100 litres chlorine-free water in a shaded drum; aerate for 24â48 hours with a small air pump; strain and dilute 1:5 with irrigation water. Apply weekly through drip lines or as a foliar spray. Always filter to 200 microns or finer to avoid emitter clogging.

Amendment N (%) P (%) K (%) Application rate
Compost tea (aerated)0.1â0.50.05â0.20.1â0.61,000â2,000 L/ha/week
Vermicompost leachate0.3â0.80.2â0.50.4â1.0500â1,000 L/ha/week
Poultry manure slurry1.5â3.01.0â2.51.0â2.0200â500 L/ha/week
Wood ash extract01.0â2.04.0â8.0100â300 L/ha/month

Source: Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), On-farm composting methods, Land and Water Discussion Paper 2, Rome, 2003; and International Water Management Institute (IWMI) research briefs on wastewater and nutrient reuse in African agriculture.

5. Irrigation for Agroforestry and Polycultures

Agroforestry systems â alley cropping, parkland trees, fruit-tree intercropping â need irrigation designed around root zones, not uniform field coverage. Practical approaches:

  • Basin irrigation around tree seedlings during establishment (first 2 dry seasons).
  • Subsurface drip at 20â30 cm depth to reach tree roots and reduce evaporation.
  • Micro-catchments (half-moons, planting pits) to capture runoff for trees.
  • Zoned scheduling: irrigate shallow-rooted intercrops more frequently than deep-rooted trees.

Polycultures with different water demands â for example, maize + pigeon pea + moringa â benefit from deficit irrigation on the cereal and full irrigation on high-value trees. This raises land-equivalent ratios and spreads market risk.

6. Reducing Energy Use in Irrigation

Energy is often the second-largest cost after labour. Practical reductions:

  • Switch from flood to drip or micro-sprinkler (30â60% energy saving).
  • Use solar PV instead of diesel or grid where feasible.
  • Irrigate at night or early morning to reduce evaporation and peak-load tariffs.
  • Maintain pumps, filters, and pipes â a 10% pressure loss can raise energy use by 15%.
  • Match pump size to system pressure; oversized pumps waste energy.
  • Use gravity where elevation allows (e.g., tank on a raised platform).
Table 2: Indicative energy and water use by irrigation method (per hectare per season)
Method Water use (mÂ³) Energy (kWh) Relative cost
Furrow / flood6,000â10,000400â900High
Sprinkler4,000â6,000300â600Medium
Drip (grid/diesel)2,500â4,000150â350Medium-low
Drip (solar)2,500â4,0000 (operating)Low (after CAPEX)

Source: Adapted from FAO, Irrigation water management: irrigation methods, Training Manual No. 5, Rome; and Global Solar Council / GIZ reports on solar irrigation in sub-Saharan Africa.

â  SAFETY WARNING â Greywater and Organic Fertigation

Never use untreated greywater or compost tea on crops eaten raw (lettuce, tomatoes, herbs) unless it has been filtered, diluted, and applied at least 2 weeks before harvest. Greywater may contain faecal coliforms, heavy metals, and detergent residues. Compost tea made from immature or contaminated compost can harbour E. coli and Salmonella. Always wear gloves and boots when handling greywater or slurry, keep children and animals away from storage tanks, and label all tanks clearly. In areas with schistosomiasis or cholera risk, consult your local public health officer before using greywater for irrigation.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Mulch every bed and install drip or micro-sprinkler lines before the dry season.
  2. Calculate dry-season water demand â not wet-season â before sizing pumps and tanks.
  3. Install first-flush diverters and 200-micron filters on all rainwater and greywater systems.
  4. Test compost tea and greywater for salinity (EC) and pH before applying to crops.
  5. Schedule irrigation for early morning or night to cut evaporation and energy costs.
  6. Service solar panels, pumps, and filters monthly; keep a simple maintenance log.
  7. Keep a 2-week pre-harvest buffer between organic fertigation and harvest for food safety.
  8. Record water, energy, and yield per hectare each season to track payback and improve decisions.

Further Reading

  • FAO â CROPWAT and irrigation water management tools
  • FAO â Small-scale irrigation for arid zones: principles and options
  • International Water Management Institute (IWMI) â research on wastewater and smallholder irrigation in Africa
  • GIZ â Solar irrigation and water pumping in Africa
  • FAO â On-farm composting methods (Land and Water Discussion Paper 2)

Business takeaway: For African smallholders, the winning combination is drip irrigation + solar pumping + organic fertigation + mulch. This package cuts water and energy costs by 40â60%, opens premium organic and export markets, and typically pays back within two to three seasons. Document every input and yield â buyers and lenders increasingly require this evidence.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of mulching in irrigation?
options: B) It reduces evaporation by up to 70%.
D) It replaces the need for water.
quiz.explanation: Mulch covers the soil and reduces evaporation, saving water.

quiz.q: Which irrigation method uses 50â70% less water than surface watering?
quiz.explanation: Olla irrigation seeps water slowly to roots, minimising waste.

quiz.q: How deep should you check soil moisture with your finger before watering?
quiz.explanation: Checking 5 cm deep gives a good indication of root-zone moisture.

quiz.q: What is a contour trench used for?
options: A) To drain water away quickly
B) To store runoff and let it soak in
quiz.explanation: Contour trenches slow runoff and increase infiltration.

quiz.q: How often should you clean drip emitters to prevent clogging?
quiz.explanation: Weekly cleaning prevents clogging and keeps water flowing evenly.

quiz.q: Which type of water is greywater?
options: B) Water from baths, sinks, and laundry
quiz.explanation: Greywater is gently used water from household sources except toilets.

quiz.q: Why should greywater not be stored for more than 24 hours?
options: B) Bacteria grow fast in warm climates.
quiz.explanation: Warm temperatures promote bacterial growth in stored greywater.

quiz.q: What is a first-flush diverter used for in rainwater harvesting?
options: B) To discard the first dirty rainwater
quiz.explanation: First-flush diverters discard the initial rain that contains dust and droppings.

quiz.q: How many litres of rainwater can a 20-square-metre roof collect in a 600 mm rainfall area per year?
quiz.explanation: 20 mÂ² Ã 0.6 m = 12 mÂ³ = 12,000 litres.

quiz.q: Which soap is safe for greywater irrigation?
quiz.explanation: Biodegradable, low-sodium soaps are safe for soil and plants.

quiz.q: What is the recommended panel size for a solar pump to irrigate 0.2 hectares of vegetables?
quiz.explanation: A 200W panel can pump about 1,500 litres per day, enough for 0.2 ha with drip.

quiz.q: Why is it better to store water in a tank than to store electricity in batteries for solar irrigation?
options: B) Batteries wear out and are expensive.
D) Water is lighter than electricity.
quiz.explanation: Batteries have limited life and high cost; storing water in a tank is more economical.

quiz.q: What is the correct tilt angle for solar panels in Malawi (latitude 13Â°S)?
quiz.explanation: In the southern hemisphere, panels should face north at an angle equal to latitude.

quiz.q: What pressure does a 1,000-litre tank at 2 metres height provide?
quiz.explanation: Each metre of height gives about 0.1 bar, so 2 m gives 0.2 bar.

quiz.q: How often should you clean solar panels to maintain output?
quiz.explanation: Dust can reduce output by 20% in a week, so weekly cleaning is needed.

quiz.q: What is compost tea?
options: B) A liquid fertiliser made by steeping compost in water
quiz.explanation: Compost tea is a nutrient-rich liquid extracted from compost.

quiz.q: How long should you steep compost in water to make compost tea?
quiz.explanation: Three days of steeping with daily stirring produces ready-to-use compost tea.

quiz.q: What dilution ratio is recommended for compost tea before application?
quiz.explanation: Diluting compost tea 1:5 with water prevents burning plants.

quiz.q: Which organic fertiliser is high in nitrogen but should not be used on young plants?
quiz.explanation: Manure tea is high in nitrogen and can burn young plants.

quiz.q: What is the safe dilution ratio for human urine as fertiliser?
quiz.explanation: Urine diluted 1:10 with water provides balanced nutrients without burning.

quiz.q: In agroforestry, which zone should be watered daily?
quiz.explanation: Zone 1 has shallow-rooted vegetables that need frequent watering.

quiz.q: What is a Zai pit?
options: B) A planting pit that captures runoff
quiz.explanation: Zai pits are dug to capture and concentrate rainwater for crops.

quiz.q: How much water does a young tree need per week in a basin irrigation system?
quiz.explanation: 20 litres per week is recommended for young trees in basins.

quiz.q: Which polyculture combination shades the soil and reduces evaporation?
quiz.explanation: Squash and beans cover the ground, reducing evaporation.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of irrigating polycultures compared to monocultures?
quiz.explanation: Diverse root systems use water at different depths, saving water.

quiz.q: What is the biggest energy cost in irrigation for smallholders?
quiz.explanation: Pumping accounts for most energy use in irrigation.

quiz.q: How can you reduce pumping energy by using gravity?
options: A) Pump water to a high tank then let it flow
B) Pump directly from the source
quiz.explanation: Storing water in an elevated tank allows gravity-fed irrigation, eliminating pumping during application.

quiz.q: What is the pressure requirement for low-pressure drip tape?
quiz.explanation: Low-pressure drip tape operates at about 0.5 bar, saving energy.

quiz.q: Why is it better to irrigate at dawn or dusk?
quiz.explanation: Cooler times reduce evaporation, so more water reaches roots.

quiz.q: What maintenance task can reduce pump energy use by 20%?
quiz.explanation: A clean impeller reduces friction and energy consumption.
